newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Kodak shares off after terse report.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kodak shares off after terse report.

text.p: The devil was in the lack of details for Eastman Kodak Co. Friday as its stock fell sharply after it issued a grim sales assessment for January and February without offering Wall Street much insight.

Kodak's stock closed at $78.50 a share, down $9.75 on the New York Stock Exchange, in heavy trading that had analysts hunting for specific reasons behind what the company said were flat sales for the period.
"They put out this cryptic announcement,"said Smith Barney analyst Peter Enderlin. "I think they probably did more harm than good."

The giant photo products company said in a brief statement that it experienced modest unit volume growth in sales in the first two months of this year, but that was offset by lower prices and the negative impact of the strong dollar.
It added that growth rates in emerging markets moderated considerably in comparison with 1996.
Kodak also said, however, that the sales report would not have a significant impact on its operations.

"Although 1997 has started more slowly than we expected, there is nothing in these first months which would cause us to change our fundamental operating plans and objectives," Chief Financial Officer Harry Kavetas said in the statement.
The company did not provide specific figures and would not specify which products or markets were affected. A spokesman said no Kodak officials would comment further.
Kodak rarely offers projections, and the fact that it offered any kind of assessment threw analysts off and sent them scurrying for more information.
"They've been rigorous about not providing any guidance, not even any winks and nods," Smith Barney's Enderlin said. "That's what made this all that surprising."
Enderlin said he has dropped his projection for Kodak's first-quarter earnings to 79 cents a share from 94 cents. Kodak earned 80 cents a share in the previous year's first quarter.
For the year, Enderlin projects earnings per share of $4.83. His previous estimate was $5.15 versus $4.50 in the prior year.
Without information from Kodak, analysts were left to speculate as to the root cause of the flat sales. Kodak would not specify which products and which parts of the country were trouble spots.

However, several analysts said they believe one weak link is Asia, where Kodak faces competition from Fuji Photo Film Co. Ltd and Konica Corp. that is additionally affected by currency issues of the dollar versus the yen.
"Mainly what's happening is slower growth and increased price competition in the Asia market," Enderlin said.
Prudential Securities analyst Alex Henderson concurred, saying currency is a significant factor in Kodak's sales for the first two months of the year.
The dollar is up 9 percent to 10 percent since Dec. 31, he said, and could hurt the company by between 40 cents and 45 cents a share on an annual basis.
"That's a big chunk of change," he said, adding that currency exchange rates are proving to be a problem for a number of multinational companies.
Henderson also said Kodak's market share was declining.
"We think they're losing considerable market share to Fuji," he said. But that speculation has not been confirmed or denied by Kodak, he noted.
Friday's announcement by Kodak did not shed any light on what might be ailing its sales.
"It was very terse," said Henderson.
